title: Are You Unknowingly Addicted to Hedges and Disclaimers
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines the habitual use of hedges and disclaimers — phrases like 'I believe' or 'from what I've seen' — that thoughtful leaders use to signal openness to other views. While occasional hedging is natural and even valuable, the author warns that leaders who hedge on nearly every statement undermine the confidence others place in them. People want leaders who acknowledge uncertainty but can still land on clear conclusions and decisions. The piece includes extensive examples of common hedges and disclaimers, and encourages readers to genuinely listen to their own speech patterns in meetings to determine whether hedging has become an unconscious default rather than a deliberate choice.
points: Hedges and disclaimers are a natural way for thoughtful leaders to signal openness to other views.
Leaders who hedge on nearly every statement, however, erode others' confidence in them over time.
People respect leaders who acknowledge uncertainty but still want them to land on clear conclusions.
The article provides extensive real examples of common hedging and disclaiming phrases leaders use.
The recommended fix is simply becoming aware of the pattern by listening to one's own speech in meetings.
quotes: Smart leaders see the gray in situations and reject the easy black-and-white answers.
So, they disclaim and hedge as a way of showing others that they have not landed on the final answer or opinion.
All leaders situate their views as less firm by disclaiming and hedging on occasion.
Leaders who inadvertently use hedges and disclaims too frequently, or all of the time, undermine the confidence others want to have in them.
Team members walk away after conversations with the sneaky feeling the leader isn’t convicted about anything, ever.
This undermines the leader’s credibility and their ability to get others to agree to a clear conclusion or decision.
